findings.title: Progress stream has no shared wire contract: per-type field subsets, hand-built frames, and a server 'error' event that collides with EventSource's transport error
findings.statement: There is one producer and two consumers of the progress stream, and no shared definition of what the stream says. In api.py::_job_event_payload each event type gets a different subset of JobState, in a different key order: progress has 4 keys, complete has 5 and error has 2. api.py::get_job_progress also writes three frames by hand, outside that builder: the 10-minute timeout and 'Job not found' frames as {"error": ...}, and, for a subscriber that arrives after another stream drained the queue, a complete frame with only status and run_id (live task 641). So the same event name 'error' carries two payload shapes, {status, message} and {error}. Each consumer reconciles them with its own fallbacks: progress-tracker.js uses `data.message || data.error`, and parameter-sweep.js uses a try/catch around JSON.parse. Naming the server event 'error' also collides with the native EventSource 'error' event that fires on a dropped connection. Both consumers add one listener for both, and progress-tracker.js::_onError and parameter-sweep.js::_followPoint then mark a still-running job 'failed' when the connection drops (live task 648). The sweep page likewise marks a point failed when the server's timeout frame arrives (live task 564). In addition, JobEvent.type is fully determined by JobState.status (running→progress, completed→complete, failed→error), so one fact is stored twice; the late-subscriber branch re-derives it inline, and the post-pin amend _FINAL_EVENT_TYPE_BY_STATUS re-derives it a third time.
findings.proposal: Define the stream once as a typed frame. JobFrame is the full asdict(JobState), with the same keys on every frame, and the event name is computed from status by one mapping, e.g. JOB_STREAM_EVENT[status] -> 'job-progress' | 'job-complete' | 'job-failed', named so it cannot collide with EventSource's 'error'. Stream-level endings (timeout, unknown job) become a distinct 'stream-closed' event whose `reason` is a Literal. Delete JobEvent.type, which is derivable, along with _job_event_payload's per-type branches and the three inline frames in get_job_progress. On the client, one module (static/js/job-stream.js: jobStream(jobId, {onState, onEnd, onDisconnected})) is the only parser, used by both progress-tracker.js and parameter-sweep.js. A transport drop then goes to onDisconnected, which keeps the last state and lets EventSource reconnect. Pin the contract with a test that asserts the frame keys equal JobState's fields. This would have prevented 641 (a late frame with different fields), 648 (a drop read as a failure), 564 (a timeout read as a failure on the sweep page), and the 533/638/649 rework that each changed one consumer.

findings.verdict_notes: Verified api.py::_job_event_payload gives per-type key subsets (4/5/2 keys); get_job_progress hand-writes {"error":...} timeout and not-found frames and a two-field complete frame for a late subscriber. progress-tracker.js uses data.message || data.error and one 'error' listener that marks failed when no data, then closes the stream; parameter-sweep.js has the same single listener. _FINAL_EVENT_TYPE_BY_STATUS is post-pin, so the 'third re-derivation' point does not apply at the pin, but the rest holds.

findings.title: Job lifecycle has no transition owner: status, finished_at and the jobs/runs rows are written independently and terminality is not guaranteed
findings.statement: A job's progress through queued→running→completed|failed is recorded as four separate facts with no legal-transition table: JobState.status, _TrackedJob.finished_at, the jobs-row status and the runs-row status. JobManager._report_state overwrites the state with whatever it is handed. Only _run_job's try/except makes a job terminal, and the executor boundary does not: JobManager._finish_job, the done-callback that runs however the future ends, stamps finished_at without checking that status is terminal. Every path that leaves _run_job's try therefore leaves a job that is finished but still 'queued' or 'running' in memory and in both rows. That covers sqlite3.connect or the PRAGMA failing before the try (live task 646), _record_failed_job's own _state_of_running_job raising inside the except, and a queued future cancelled by shutdown(cancel_futures=True). An SSE stream on that job then heartbeats until its 10-minute cap, and the job silently ages out after _FINISHED_JOB_TTL_SECONDS. Run status also has two writers that can reverse each other. RunStorage.save_home_run/save_fleet_run upsert the run as 'completed' inside work_fn. If the following _record_completed_job UPDATE raises (for example 'database is locked' with two workers), the except branch's _record_failed_run_row turns that completed run, whose files are on disk, into 'failed'. That completed→failed transition is illegal, and nothing refuses it.
findings.proposal: Introduce a JobLifecycle with a single writer, JobManager._transition(job_id, new_state). It checks LEGAL_JOB_TRANSITIONS = {queued: {running, failed}, running: {running, completed, failed}}. An illegal move raises an error naming the job, the old status and the new one, and terminal states are final. Make terminality a property of the executor boundary: _finish_job reads future.exception() / future.cancelled(), and if the tracked status is not terminal it transitions the job to failed, with the escaped exception or 'dropped by shutdown' as the message. With that in place _run_job's try/except no longer has to be exhaustive, and the 646 class cannot recur. Run status should follow the job: either RunStorage's save stops writing status and the lifecycle writes 'completed' after the save, or the lifecycle skips the failed write once the run is completed. The legality check also removes the completed→failed overwrite. recover_stale_jobs should be expressed through the same table (queued|running → failed).
findings.bug_history_link: fix(552) 9899648 (its message lists 'raised before _run_job's try, or dropped by shutdown' as paths that only get finished_at); amend 615360b; fix(627) 25860e1; fix(132) ae91b49; live 646 (already filed: exception before _run_job's try lost in an unread Future)
findings.verdict_notes: _finish_job only stamps finished_at and never checks status is terminal. _run_job runs sqlite3.connect and the PRAGMA before its try. shutdown uses cancel_futures=True (jobs.py:227). _record_failed_job calls _state_of_running_job outside any guard, inside the except path. No transition table exists.

findings.title: A stored run's summary is an untyped dict whose home/fleet key set every reader guesses
findings.statement: save_home_run writes summary_json from SummaryStatistics and save_fleet_run writes it from FleetSummary, and the two key sets differ. For example, FleetSummary has fleet_self_consumption_ratio and no self_consumption_ratio, grid_dependency_ratio or total_battery_charge_kwh. Yet RunRecord.decoded_summary returns Any, and the run's `type` never selects a schema on the way out. At least six readers read home keys by string. api.history_list_runs and assistant.list_recent_runs read summary.get('self_consumption_ratio'), which is None for every fleet run (live 653). charts.comparison_radar, reached from history.compare_page, reads self_consumption_ratio, grid_dependency_ratio and total_battery_charge_kwh with default 0, so fleets draw at 0% (live 565, 654). routes._get_aggregate_stats reads json_extract(summary_json,'$.total_generation_kwh'), which works for both types only because the two key sets happen to share that name. parameter-sweep.js reads s.self_consumption_ratio from api.get_job_results. There are also three decoders of the same text with different failure behaviour. RunRecord.decoded_summary swallows a decode error and returns {}. api.get_job_results calls json.loads and raises, giving a 500. assistant.get_run_results calls json.loads and the error is caught as a 'Database error'.
findings.proposal: Make the decoded summary typed and tagged by run type. RunRecord.summary() -> SummaryStatistics | FleetSummary | None dispatches on self.type through the existing _deserialize_dataclass. Add a frozen RunHeadline (generation_kwh, self_consumption_ratio, grid_import_kwh, battery_charge_kwh | None, ...) built by one function, run_headline(summary), which matches on the summary type. That function is the only place that knows fleet_self_consumption_ratio corresponds to self_consumption_ratio. History list, assistant list/get, aggregate stats, get_job_results (and so the sweep page) and the compare charts serialize RunHeadline and stop calling .get on raw keys. With every reader on it, the string-key reads and the json_extract key become deletable, as do the three ad-hoc json.loads paths. A missing headline field becomes a type error in one function rather than a null in four pages. This would have prevented 653, 565, 654 and the 410 rounding/summary drift.
findings.bug_history_link: live 653, 565, 654, 575, 547; fix(410) e4a85ff/1133e58; amend 8f36401 (shared decoding added but still Any)
findings.verdict_notes: decoded_summary returns Any and swallows errors into {}. api.py:270 and assistant.py:510/562 use bare json.loads. api.py:703, assistant.py:573 and charts.py:746 read self_consumption_ratio by string with no run-type dispatch.

findings.title: The jobs table is a write-only mirror of in-memory job state, and most of jobs.py's consistency churn maintains it
findings.statement: No production code reads the jobs table. A grep of src/ finds only jobs.py's own INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, and JobManager.job_state's docstring says the manager 'never reads the jobs table'. recover_stale_jobs only UPDATEs it and uses rowcount for a log line, while the runs rows are recovered by their own status. Even so, every transition writes it: one INSERT, an UPDATE plus commit on each progress tick (a fleet emits one per home), a second UPDATE just for started_at, the completed UPDATE, the failed UPDATE with error_traceback, which is never shown anywhere, and the DELETE in _forget_job. _run_job opens a sqlite3 connection before its try only to carry these writes. Neither runner's work_fn uses the `conn` it is passed, because RunStorage opens its own. That connection is the pre-try code of live task 646. So job state lives in two stores, one of them never read, and keeping them consistent produced a run of fixes and amends: 543 (track only after both rows are written), 627 (per-row transactions and logging), amends 06eaa8d, 45ea53f and 78c64c6, and 6e82f01 (_forget_job deletes the rows of a refused job).
findings.proposal: Pick one home for a job's state. The briefing already makes the in-memory JobManager authoritative for live jobs, and the runs row is the durable record of the outcome. Under that choice, delete the jobs-table writes: the jobs INSERT in _record_new_job, the UPDATEs in _update_progress, _run_job's started_at UPDATE, _record_completed_job's UPDATE, _record_failed_job_row, the jobs DELETE in _forget_job and the jobs UPDATE in recover_stale_jobs. Then delete _run_job's connection and work_fn's unused conn parameter, and drop the table (database.py has no migrations, so the table can simply stop being created). If a durable job record is actually wanted, for example so /api/jobs/<id> answers after the 1 h TTL, make job_state fall back to the table so it has a reader. Either way, every write gets a reader or is deleted.

findings.verdict_notes: grep of src finds jobs-table INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE only in jobs.py, with no SELECT. The job_state docstring says the manager never reads it. _run_job opens a conn before its try, and the work_fn closures build their own RunStorage (jobs.py:656, 723).

findings.title: The runs table has no single owner: its row shape, status writes and queries are restated across jobs.py, api.py, routes.py and assistant.py
findings.statement: RunStorage derives its runs upsert from RunRecord's fields (storage.py::_run_row_upsert, added by task 577 to stop the INSERT being restated). JobManager._record_new_job still restates the same 12-column INSERT positionally, with inline None comments. Run status has two writers: RunStorage's upsert writes 'completed', and jobs.py writes 'running' at insert, 'failed' in _record_failed_run_row and in recover_stale_jobs, and deletes in _forget_job. Reads also bypass RunStorage. api.history_list_runs builds its own WHERE/ORDER/LIMIT query, which duplicates RunStorage.list_runs' filtering with a different filter set. routes._get_aggregate_stats has a function-local get_db import and a literal status = 'completed'. assistant.list_recent_runs runs its own SELECT. Each of these restates the column set and the status vocabulary outside the RunStatus Literal's reach. One stated fact goes unenforced: RunType declares 'sweep', and runs.html offers a 'Sweep' filter, but no writer ever stores type 'sweep'. Sweep points are saved as 'home' runs named 'Sweep x=y', so that filter always returns nothing. JobManager also takes db_path/data_dir on every submit and builds a new RunStorage per job instead of using the app's one.
findings.proposal: Make RunStorage the only module that issues SQL against runs, and inject it into JobManager (JobManager(storage=...)) so submits stop carrying db_path/data_dir. Move the remaining operations into RunStorage: create_queued_run(id, name, type, n_homes, created_at), built from RunRecord like the upsert; mark_run_failed(id, message, at); forget_run(id); fail_interrupted_runs(); a page_runs(filter: RunQuery) that returns RunRecords plus a total, replacing both history_list_runs' SQL and list_runs; and aggregate_stats(). Status values come from RunStatus constants. Deletable: the INSERT in _record_new_job, _record_failed_run_row's SQL, the SQL in api.history_list_runs, routes._get_aggregate_stats and assistant.list_recent_runs, plus routes.py's function-local get_db import. Either write 'sweep' runs or delete 'sweep' from RunType and the filter option.

findings.verdict_notes: _record_new_job restates a positional 12-column runs INSERT with inline None comments. routes._get_aggregate_stats has a function-local get_db import. RunStorage is built per job in jobs.py. Sweep points are submitted via submit_home_job as 'Sweep x=y' (api.py:592), and no writer stores type 'sweep', though runs.html offers the filter.

findings.title: get_events is a destructive single-consumer queue, but a job's progress stream has several subscribers
findings.statement: Each _TrackedJob has one deque (maxlen=100) of JobEvents, and JobManager.get_events copies and clears it under the lock. Whichever caller drains first therefore consumes the events, even though the method's name says 'get' (live 680). A job's stream regularly has more than one subscriber: EventSource reconnects automatically, a second tab or a page reload opens a new stream, and the sweep page and the results page can follow the same job. The consumers need the latest state, not a log: every frame carries a full JobState snapshot, and progress is idempotent. Because a second subscriber finds the queue empty, api.get_job_progress needs a compensating branch that rebuilds a terminal frame from job_state, and that branch is where the 641 two-field complete frame came from. It also has to read job_state and drain events in two separate lock holds and reason about the race between them.
findings.proposal: Replace the event queue with a versioned snapshot. _TrackedJob keeps state plus a monotonically increasing version, bumped by _report_state, and the manager exposes a non-destructive job_snapshot(job_id) -> (version, JobState). Each stream keeps its own cursor and emits a frame whenever the version moves, ending when the snapshot's status is terminal. Deletable: _TrackedJob.events, JobEvent's queue role, get_events, and get_job_progress's late-subscriber terminal branch. Multiple subscribers, reconnects and late subscribers all get the same frames, which removes the bug class behind 641 and 680.
findings.bug_history_link: live 680 (already filed: get_events drains while named as a read), 641 (late-subscriber frame); fix(533) b366f18
findings.verdict_notes: get_events copies and clears job.events under the lock (jobs.py:376-377). get_job_progress reads job_state and then drains events in separate lock holds, with a compensating terminal-state branch.

findings.title: Request values are coerced per field at each endpoint, with silent defaults, instead of parsed into typed request records at the boundary
findings.statement: Only the outer object has a shared rule at the boundary: shared.require_json_object, which task 249 introduced and which maps to 400 through the blueprint's NotAJsonObject handler. Fields are read ad hoc. api.simulate_fleet_api passes data.get('name') unchecked into JobManager.submit_fleet_job and on to the runs INSERT, so a non-string name raises sqlite3's ProgrammingError and answers 500 (live 517, together with parse_home_config's unchecked params['name']). api.simulate_sweep reads mode with str(data.get('mode')) and treats any value other than 'geometric', including a typo, as linear, although its docstring lists only 'linear' | 'geometric'. parse_home_config reads bool(params['stochastic']), so the string 'false' runs the stochastic model. shared.resolve_location turns an unrecognised location into Bristol. api.py has five per-endpoint `except (ValueError, TypeError) -> 400` blocks, each catching whatever its own coercions happen to raise. Under this structure each new field is another chance of a 500 or a silent default (14 mined fixes: 165, 243, 249/268, 435, 557, 339; live 331, 517, 560).
findings.proposal: Parse each request body once into a frozen request record (HomeRunRequest, FleetRunRequest, SweepRequest with mode: Literal['linear','geometric']) using one parse_request(cls, body) helper. The helper refuses wrong JSON types, unknown Literal values and over-long strings by raising a single RequestRefused(field, value, expected) error, and the api blueprint's errorhandler maps it to 400 as it already does for NotAJsonObject. JobManager.submit_* then take the typed record. Deletable: the five ad-hoc except blocks, the str()/bool()/float() coercions in simulate_sweep and parse_home_config, and the silent fallbacks. Recurrence of 517, 331 and 560 is then structurally ruled out.
findings.verdict_notes: Verified: data.get('name') is unchecked, mode is str(data.get('mode','linear')) with a silent linear fallback, bool(params['stochastic']) is in simulation_params.py, and the except blocks are per-endpoint. The cited task count (14 fixes) and the 500 on a non-string name are only partly checked, and the outer-object rule (request_json_object) is real. The pattern is real but the framing as a systemic missing invariant is somewhat broad.

findings.title: resolve_location turns any unrecognised location into Bristol without saying so
findings.statement: shared.py::resolve_location maps a preset name or a 'lat,lon' string to a Location. For anything else, such as 'Paris', 'lodnon' or '51.5;-0.1', it catches ValueError and returns Location.bristol(). The same happens to an out-of-range 'lat,lon', because Location's own ValueError is caught too. The simulation then runs, and is saved and reported, for Bristol while the request named somewhere else, with no 400 and no warning. The assistant's run_home_simulation tool passes model-written location strings through the same path, so a model's typo produces a plausible-looking result for the wrong place. The function's name says it resolves the location it is given, which it does not do in this case.
findings.proposal: Raise a ValueError that names the value and the accepted forms (the LOCATION_PRESETS keys, or 'lat,lon'), and let it propagate. parse_home_config's callers already answer ValueError with 400, and the assistant tools already turn it into an {error} dict. Delete the Bristol fallback.
findings.bug_history_link: speculative
findings.verdict_notes: resolve_location catches ValueError, including an out-of-range Location's, and returns Location.bristol(). Its docstring says 'Falls back to Bristol on parse errors', so the behaviour is documented but silent. The consequence is a wrong-place result with no 400.

findings.title: 'Finite, non-negative physical quantity' is re-spelled per class in three polarities, and the flow entry points validate nothing
findings.statement: There is no shared definition of a valid physical quantity. Each class spells its own comparison, in three incompatible polarities. (a) NaN-permissive: `if x < 0` / `if x <= 0`. dispatch.py has 21 such guards: DispatchDecision.__post_init__ x3, the same five-check input block copied into each of the three decide_action methods x15, compute_grid_charge_power_kw, PeakShavingStrategy.__init__. heat_pump.py::HeatPumpConfig has 2 and ev.py::EVConfig has 1. (b) NaN-refusing but inf-accepting: `not x >= 0` in flow.py::EnergyFlowResult.__post_init__ and battery.py::_require_valid_request. (c) Fully finite: `not 0 < x < math.inf` in battery.py::BatteryConfig and require_valid_power_limit, and in load.py::LoadConfig. flow.py::simulate_timestep and simulate_timestep_tou check none of their own inputs (generation_kw, demand_kw, timestep_minutes). Whether a bad value is refused depends on which path runs, whether a battery is present, and which downstream object happens to look. docs/domain-library-consumption.md needs one paragraph per fix (590, 633) just to enumerate which path now refuses what. Probed at the pin, all of these are accepted: HeatPumpConfig('ASHP', nan, nan); EVConfig('7kW', 18, required_charge_kwh=nan); DispatchDecision(nan, 0.0); PeakShavingStrategy(nan) (task 673). simulate_timestep(inf, 1.0, None) returns generation=inf and grid_export=inf (tasks 659, 672). The only reusable finite-number helper, web/number_fields.py::as_finite_float, lives in the web layer, above the domain that needs it.
findings.proposal: Add a dependency-free domain module src/solar_challenge/quantities.py with three checkers: require_finite_at_least(name, value, low, *, inclusive), require_fraction(name, value, *, open_low, open_high) and require_positive_finite(name, value). Each raises ValueError naming the quantity, its value and the bound, which satisfies INV-2. Every __post_init__ in battery/dispatch/flow/heat_pump/ev/load calls them. That rewrites the 21 dispatch guards, HeatPumpConfig, EVConfig, and EnergyFlowResult (which also refuses inf). battery.require_valid_power_limit and require_valid_capacity_setting stay public, as one-line delegations because of the frozen surface. Give flow.simulate_timestep and simulate_timestep_tou one shared entry check, _require_timestep_inputs(generation_kw, demand_kw, timestep_minutes), so behaviour no longer depends on the path. The five-check block copied into each decide_action collapses into one dispatch-module helper the three strategies call. They keep it because consumers call strategies directly. web/number_fields.as_finite_float delegates to quantities.py. Add a unit test that AST-scans src/solar_challenge for `raise ValueError` guarded by a bare `<`/`<=` comparison against a literal and fails, naming the site, so the polarity cannot regress. This removes the bug class of tasks 378, 590, 633, 659, 672 and 673 and the unfiled HeatPumpConfig/EVConfig NaN acceptance.

findings.verdict_notes: Probed at the pin: HeatPumpConfig('ASHP',nan,nan), EVConfig(required_charge_kwh=nan), DispatchDecision(nan,0.0) and PeakShavingStrategy(nan) are all accepted. simulate_timestep(inf,1.0,None) returns generation=inf and grid_export=inf. simulate_timestep and simulate_timestep_tou check none of their own inputs. battery.py::_require_valid_request uses `not power_kw >= 0` and a finite-duration check, and BatteryConfig uses `0 < x < math.inf`; the polarities differ.

findings.title: The battery's SOC envelope (SOH-derated capacity, kWh limits) is owned only by the stateful Battery, so consumers re-derive it or use nominal capacity
findings.statement: The battery has five capacity concepts and no single value owns them. (1) BatteryConfig.capacity_kwh is nominal. (2) BatteryConfig.nominal_usable_capacity_kwh uses the config's SOC fractions, not a Battery's overridden ones. (3) SOH is resolved only inside Battery.__init__: the override wins, otherwise compute_soh with throughput fixed at 0.0. finance.py::_aged_homes runs compute_soh separately and injects the result as config.soh. (4) Battery.effective_capacity_kwh, min_soc_kwh and max_soc_kwh exist only on the mutable, stateful Battery. (5) The grid-charge target is measured against nominal capacity. flow.py::simulate_timestep passes battery.config.capacity_kwh as decide_action's battery_capacity_kwh, documented as 'Total battery capacity', and simulate_timestep_tou passes it as compute_grid_charge_power_kw's capacity_kwh. compute_grid_charge_power_kw then computes target_kwh = target_soc_fraction x nominal, while Battery clamps the SOC at a fraction of SoH-derated capacity. Probe: BatteryConfig(capacity_kwh=10, soh=0.6) has max_soc_kwh=5.4, while the default 0.9 target asks for 9 kWh, so the controller never sees the gap close (task 632). Any reader that needs the derated limits must construct a throwaway Battery: web/charts.py::battery_soc_chart (the task 645 fix) and gridservices.py::compute_fleet_spare_capacity_kw (Battery(battery_config).min_soc_kwh). A reader that does not know this uses nominal figures, as the chart did before 645.
findings.proposal: Add a frozen value battery.py::SocEnvelope(effective_capacity_kwh, min_soc_kwh, max_soc_kwh). One pure function builds it: BatteryConfig.soc_envelope(*, min_soc_fraction=None, max_soc_fraction=None), which also does the single SOH resolution (override or compute_soh), moved out of Battery.__init__. Battery holds the envelope, recomputes it when an SOC-fraction setter fires, and derives min/max_soc_kwh, usable_capacity_kwh and available_* from it. charts.battery_soc_chart and gridservices.compute_fleet_spare_capacity_kw call config.soc_envelope() and stop instantiating Battery. Flow passes envelope-derived capacity to strategies and the grid-charge controller. compute_grid_charge_power_kw clamps target_kwh to the envelope's max_soc_kwh. Signatures stay frozen; only the documented meaning of battery_capacity_kwh changes, under the release note. Record the rule 'every capacity a dispatcher sees is SoH-derated' as one invariant in battery.py, and pin it with a test that runs a derated battery through both flow paths. This closes 632 and the class of 645, and stops the next consumer from picking the wrong capacity.

findings.verdict_notes: flow.py::simulate_timestep passes battery.config.capacity_kwh as battery_capacity_kwh. simulate_timestep_tou passes it as capacity_kwh to compute_grid_charge_power_kw, which computes target_kwh = fraction * nominal. Probe: BatteryConfig(capacity_kwh=10, soh=0.6) gives Battery.max_soc_kwh=5.4 and nominal_usable_capacity_kwh=8.0, while the 0.9 target is 9 kWh. web/charts.py:216 and gridservices.py:446 each build a throwaway Battery to read the derated limits.

findings.title: The one-shot DispatchStrategy cannot express the rate-aware path's charge-then-top-up, so flow.py keeps a second executor and a duplicated settle tail
findings.statement: This finding takes the briefing's key decision to keep two dispatch behaviours as given. The mechanism, not the behaviour, is what is duplicated. DispatchStrategy.decide_action returns one decision computed from the pre-step SOC. The rate-aware path needs PV charging to land first and the grid top-up to be sized from the post-PV SOC. That sequencing does not fit the interface, so flow.py::simulate_timestep_tou decides and executes inline with interleaved battery.charge calls. It then repeats the same 27-line settle tail as simulate_timestep: battery_charge sum, direct and self-consumption, split-source export/import, EnergyFlowResult construction, and an identical 7-line comment (task 270). As a result the 'shared' grid-charge controller is fed different inputs on the two paths. simulate_timestep_tou passes post-PV-charge SOC and pv_charge_power_kw = min(excess, max_charge_kw). The strategy path, via TOUOptimizedStrategy/PeakShavingStrategy.decide_action, passes pre-step SOC and an unclamped charge_kw. So with excess PV in a cheap period, the strategy path sizes the grid draw as if no PV were stored and overshoots the target, while the TOU path does not. The two strategies also each carry a copy of the 15-line grid-charge gate block. EnergyFlowResult accepts caller-computed derived flows, so energy balance is checked after the fact by validate_energy_balance, which callers can switch off and which reads six of eight flows. It is never true by construction.
findings.proposal: Add one pure settle function in flow.py, _settle(generation_kwh, demand_kwh, pv_stored_kwh, grid_stored_kwh, discharged_kwh, soc_kwh) -> EnergyFlowResult, as the only producer of derived flows. Both paths call it, the duplicated tail and its comment are deleted (task 270), and the result balances by construction; validate_energy_balance stays as a redundant check. Then add one executor, _execute(decision, battery, minutes) -> (pv_stored, grid_stored, discharged). Express the rate-aware path as a two-phase decision (PV phase, then grid phase sized from the post-PV SOC) through the same executor, keeping its behaviour. Have the strategy path size grid charge from the SOC after PV in the same way, so compute_grid_charge_power_kw sees the same SOC basis on both paths. Move the copied grid-charge gate in TOUOptimizedStrategy and PeakShavingStrategy into one module helper, _grid_charge_kw(ctx, soc, capacity, charge_kw, discharge_kw, minutes). A dispatch change is then made once.
findings.bug_history_link: live 270 (27-line tail); f8004c9 amend: extract _is_cheap_period helper to eliminate cheap-period duplication (an earlier patch of the same split); 3ebc5f3/397bc09 grid-charge wired into each strategy separately
findings.verdict_notes: The settle tail (battery_charge sum through the EnergyFlowResult construction, with its comment block) is duplicated line for line in simulate_timestep and simulate_timestep_tou. The TOU path passes post-PV-charge SOC and a clamped pv_charge_power_kw. TOUOptimizedStrategy and PeakShavingStrategy pass pre-step SOC and the unclamped charge_kw, and each carries its own copy of the grid-charge gate block. Both the duplication and the input mismatch are real.

findings.title: Dispatch selection is two unvalidated or partly validated strings in two vocabularies, routed by if/elif in home.py and restated in config.py
findings.statement: Which dispatcher a home runs is decided by two string fields with different vocabularies. HomeConfig.dispatch_strategy: str ('greedy' or 'tou_optimized') has no __post_init__, so HomeConfig(dispatch_strategy='peak_shaving') or any typo silently runs self-consumption. BatteryConfig.dispatch_strategy is a DispatchStrategyConfig whose strategy_type: str is checked against a local tuple. The vocabularies are restated in config.py::_VALID_DISPATCH_STRATEGIES, the tuple in DispatchStrategyConfig.__post_init__, the if/elif in home.py::_create_dispatch_strategy (which re-checks peak_hours and import_limit_kw, already refused by the config because DispatchStrategyConfig is a mutable @dataclass), and the strategies' name properties. The precedence rule (tariff TOU only when the battery has no strategy, and only with a tariff) lives in simulate_home's use_tariff_tou. It is restated as a warning in config.py::_read_fleet_distribution_file and had to be documented side by side in 5e0f953. 'tou_optimized' names two different mechanisms, and simulate_home hard-codes strategy_name='tou_optimized' for the tariff path, so results cannot say which one ran. import_limit_kw's positivity is checked twice, both times NaN-permissive (task 673).
findings.proposal: Replace the routing with one resolver in home.py (or dispatch.py), resolve_dispatch(home_config) -> DispatchPlan. DispatchPlan is a frozen sum type: either StrategyDispatch(strategy) or TariffTouDispatch(tariff), each with a distinct result name such as 'tou_optimized' and 'tou_rate_aware'. It is the only place the precedence and the no-tariff fallback are decided. config.py's warning calls it instead of restating the rule. Give HomeConfig a __post_init__ that validates dispatch_strategy against the single vocabulary, moved out of config.py's _VALID_DISPATCH_STRATEGIES. Freeze DispatchStrategyConfig and give it a to_strategy() method, so _create_dispatch_strategy's if/elif and its re-checks are deleted. Widening the fields to Enums is the follow-up that needs the frozen-surface version bump. This stops the class seen in 340/519/335 where each reader re-learns how the two keys relate.
findings.bug_history_link: 3825268/a3b6c23 (340) battery-level dispatch_strategy; fd0c3da fix(519) web form refuses battery-level dispatch_strategy; 5e0f953 amend: document how the two dispatch_strategy keys relate; fdef0cd refactor(335); live 673
findings.verdict_notes: HomeConfig is a frozen dataclass with `dispatch_strategy: str = "greedy"` and no __post_init__. _create_dispatch_strategy re-checks peak_hours and import_limit_kw, which DispatchStrategyConfig already refuses. config.py has the separate _VALID_DISPATCH_STRATEGIES frozenset({'greedy','tou_optimized'}) and the tuple in DispatchStrategyConfig.__post_init__. simulate_home hard-codes strategy_name='tou_optimized' on the tariff-TOU path. I did not check the exact commit hashes cited.

findings.title: A battery's max_charge_kw is a per-call clamp, but simulate_timestep calls charge twice per step, so a consumer strategy can charge at twice the limit
findings.statement: Battery.charge clamps each call's power to config.max_charge_kw. flow.py::simulate_timestep executes a decision with two calls: battery.charge(decision.charge_kw, ...) and then battery.charge(decision.grid_charge_kw, ...). DispatchDecision.__post_init__ does not bound charge_kw + grid_charge_kw. The built-in strategies keep the sum under the limit only through compute_grid_charge_power_kw's residual arithmetic. DispatchStrategy is a frozen extension point that consumers implement. Probe at the pin: with a strategy returning DispatchDecision(charge_kw=5, discharge_kw=0, grid_charge_kw=5) against BatteryConfig(capacity_kwh=10, max_charge_kw=2.5), one 60-minute step stores 4.875 kWh, which is twice the hardware limit times efficiency. The per-step power invariant belongs to the battery but is enforced by caller arithmetic.
findings.proposal: Make the battery own the per-step limit. Add Battery.charge_split(pv_kw, grid_kw, duration_minutes) -> (pv_stored_kwh, grid_stored_kwh), which clamps pv_kw + grid_kw to max_charge_kw once, giving PV priority. simulate_timestep and simulate_timestep_tou use it. Alternatively, flow clamps grid_charge_kw to max(0, max_charge_kw - min(charge_kw, max_charge_kw)) before the second call. Add a test with a consumer strategy over the limit.
findings.bug_history_link: speculative (unfiled; probed at 7dfea36)
findings.verdict_notes: Probe reproduced it exactly: a strategy returning DispatchDecision(charge_kw=5, discharge_kw=0, grid_charge_kw=5) on BatteryConfig(capacity_kwh=100, max_charge_kw=2.5) over one 60-minute step stores battery_charge=4.875 kWh. That is two clamped charge calls, twice the per-step limit. The finding's own 10 kWh example is capped by the SOC maximum, but the claim holds with headroom.

findings.title: The EV profile is indexed by positional minutes from the window start, so its charging times depend on the window and a DST-crossing window gains an hour
findings.statement: The simulation's minute index is built in three places with two rules. load.py::_generate_elexon_profile and _try_richardsonpy_profile build a DST-aware wall-clock index (start .. end+1d-1min, freq 1min, tz), each with its own copy of a trim/pad block. ev.py::generate_ev_charging_profile instead builds n_days*1440 positional minutes from start_date and places charging by minute offset within each 1440-block. load.py::generate_load_profile combines them with base_load.add(ev_load, fill_value=0.0), which takes the union of the indexes and hides any mismatch. Probed at the pin with LoadConfig(3400, use_stochastic=False) and EVConfig('7kW', arrival_hour=18). Over 2024-03-30..2024-04-01 the base load has 4260 rows ending 2024-04-01 23:59+01:00, while the combined demand has 4320 rows ending 2024-04-02 00:59+01:00: 60 minutes past the requested window, which simulate_home then simulates. For a full-year 2024 run, the EV's first charging minute on 21 June is 19:00+01:00, but 18:00+01:00 for a one-day 21 June run. The same home on the same date charges an hour later depending on the window start, which mis-times EV demand for every BST day of an annual run. This is the timebase-seam class of tasks 166 and 190.
findings.proposal: Add one constructor of the simulation index to timebase.py, minute_index(start, end, tz) -> DatetimeIndex. Each generator takes the index rather than start/end: the Elexon path, the richardsonpy path, the EV path and pv's minute expansion. Each generator places per-day values by wall-clock minute-of-day (index.hour*60+index.minute), not by position, so both trim/pad blocks are deleted. generate_load_profile adds components only after asserting index equality, failing with the two lengths and endpoints instead of fill_value=0.0. Add a test that runs one EV home over a DST-crossing window and over a full year, and pins the window length and the 18:00 local arrival on a BST day.
findings.bug_history_link: speculative (unfiled; probed at 7dfea36); same seam as f205230 fix(166) and 349740b fix(190); 38c84ed amend: fix DST off-by-one in window_days
findings.verdict_notes: The EV profile is built from n_days*1440 positional minutes (ev.py). Probe over 2024-03-30..2024-04-01: base load has 4260 rows ending 04-01 23:59+01:00, combined has 4320 rows ending 04-02 00:59+01:00. The EV charge on 21 June starts at 19:00+01:00 in a full-year run and 18:00+01:00 in a one-day run. load.py::generate_load_profile combines the two series with a fill_value union.

findings.title: simulate_home composes household demand inline, while EV demand is composed inside load.py: one additive-load axis, two mechanisms, and the time-alignment fixes land in a 180-line function
findings.statement: home.py::simulate_home (about 180 lines) does nine jobs: weather fetch and year-length check, PV simulation and expansion, base and EV load (delegated), heat-pump temperature alignment and load composition (inline), battery construction, dispatch routing, the timestep loop, tariff and SEG pricing, and results assembly. The 'additional household load' axis has two mechanisms. EV load is folded in inside load.generate_load_profile through a function-local import and a fill_value union. Heat-pump load is folded in inside simulate_home, with its own UTC TMY alignment and an annual-year check. That check is spelled twice: _YEAR_LENGTHS_IN_HOURS in home.py and _YEAR_LENGTHS_IN_MINUTES in heat_pump.py, both from reference_year_lengths, which lives in heat_pump.py although it describes the TMY. Every fix at this seam (166 UTC alignment, 168 series naming, 190 leap day, 206 annual-demand sharing) had to be made inside simulate_home, and 276 had to repeat 168's naming fix inside heat_pump.py. A new load component (e.g. a second EV, storage heating) has no obvious home.
findings.proposal: Create src/solar_challenge/demand.py with household_demand(config, weather_year, index) -> HouseholdDemand. HouseholdDemand is a frozen value with base_kw, ev_kw, heat_pump_kw and total_kw, all on the one timebase.minute_index from the EV finding, with each component's series name fixed there. It owns TMY-to-index alignment for temperature and the reference-year check, and reference_year_lengths moves to weather.py beside align_tmy_to_index. simulate_home shrinks to weather, PV, demand, dispatch loop and pricing, with pricing extracted as _price_results(results_list, index, tariff, seg). generate_load_profile keeps its frozen ev_config parameter as a delegation to the same composition.
findings.verdict_notes: simulate_home spans lines 292-475, about 183 lines. EV load is composed in load.py through a function-local import at line 447. The heat pump is composed inline in simulate_home, which also holds a year-length check against home.py::_YEAR_LENGTHS_IN_HOURS; heat_pump.py has a second check on _YEAR_LENGTHS_IN_MINUTES. Both derive from heat_pump.py::reference_year_lengths, so the shared derivation makes the 'spelled twice' point slightly overstated.

findings.title: The stochastic load generator is a 170-line function under a blanket except, and its tests patch load's private day simulator and richardsonpy's internals
findings.statement: load.py::_try_richardsonpy_profile (about 170 lines) does all of the following: resolves richardsonpy's data-file paths, seeds global RNGs, normalises dates, builds occupancy, loops over days, trims or pads for DST (a copy of _generate_elexon_profile's block), and scales to the seasonal target. All of it sits inside `except Exception` that logs and returns None, so a defect in the project's own code (e.g. a ValueError in the scaling) silently switches the model to the deterministic Elexon shape. The only seam is the module-private _simulate_stochastic_day. tests/unit/test_load.py::TestWindowedStochasticGeneration reaches it with monkeypatch.setattr(load_module, '_simulate_stochastic_day', ...) to exercise the fallback. Its window-count tests patch richardsonpy's own run_application_simulation to count calls, which pins third-party internals, not behaviour.
findings.proposal: Extract a narrow adapter, a RichardsonpyDaySource class with one method day_kw(date, occupants) -> ndarray, built once per profile. _try_richardsonpy_profile becomes a short loop over minute_index days that calls the adapter and then a shared _scale_to_seasonal_target. Narrow the except to wrap only the adapter calls, so the project's own errors propagate. Tests inject a fake day source through a keyword-only parameter of a module-level helper the public path calls, which removes both monkeypatches.
findings.bug_history_link: 2180d5f fix(load): windowed stochastic generation; 38c84ed amend: fix DST off-by-one in window_days; dbc1758 amend: log fallback warning
findings.verdict_notes: Real: the function spans lines 228-400, about 170 lines, with a blanket `except Exception` and a function-local richardsonpy import. tests/unit/test_load.py:547 monkeypatches load_module._simulate_stochastic_day, and other tests monkeypatch richardsonpy's run_application_simulation. Overstated: the fallback is not silent. The except block calls logger.warning with the exception type and message, so the 'silently' claim is wrong.

findings.title: PVConfig fields that the default model path never reads, one guarded by a sentinel comparison
findings.statement: PVConfig.module_efficiency is validated in __post_init__ but is read nowhere in pv.py; the only module-building function that accepts an efficiency, create_simple_module_params, is not fed from PVConfig. _module_parameters applies temperature_coefficient only through the sentinel test `config.temperature_coefficient != -0.004`, and writes it to gamma_pdc on a CEC catalogue module, where pvlib's single-diode model reads gamma_r (live task 195). When custom_module_params is set, temperature_coefficient and module_efficiency are dropped silently. Yet both fields are parsed from YAML, sampled as fleet distributions (config.py::generate_homes_from_distribution samples module_efficiency per home), written back by scenario_writer, and offered as sweep or distribution axes. Users can therefore vary module efficiency across a fleet and get identical output. This is the same shape as the task 236 defect, a default value doubling as 'keep the catalogue value', and no check ties a PVConfig field to the path that consumes it. Because each parameter is checked at construction but never at use, the next unread field will not be caught either.
findings.proposal: Make the module choice one typed value resolved at construction. Introduce a frozen module spec in pv.py (catalogue module / PVWatts module with rating_w and gamma_pdc / custom parameters) and have PVConfig carry that instead of the loose module_efficiency, temperature_coefficient and custom_module_params trio. Enforce applicability in one place, PVConfig.__post_init__ and the module resolver: a field the chosen path ignores must be absent or refused, with an error naming the field and the path. Either wire the CEC path properly (gamma_r and efficiency into the single-diode parameters, with a measurement as for 203/236) or remove the two fields from the scenario grammar and distributions. This deletes the `!= -0.004` sentinel, the dead module_efficiency distribution plumbing, and the 'ignored when custom' footgun, and would have prevented tasks 195 and 236 and the 196 chain mismatch.

findings.verdict_notes: pv.py::PVConfig validates module_efficiency in __post_init__ but no other pv.py use. _module_parameters applies temperature_coefficient only when != -0.004, writing gamma_pdc, and returns custom_module_params untouched. config.py samples module_efficiency per home (generate_homes_from_distribution) and scenario_writer::_pv_block writes it, so the field is varied with no effect.

findings.title: The PV physics is split between the model chain and simulate_pv_output
findings.statement: System losses are a step inside the pvlib ModelChain (_deduct_system_losses, DC side), while ageing and the non-negative clip are applied after the chain, on AC, by simulate_pv_output (apply_degradation(ac_power, ...)). The public create_model_chain therefore returns a chain that does not age, and simulate_pv_output returns something the chain cannot produce. Two entry points disagree about what 'the PV model' is, and the measurement scripts use both (create_model_chain at scripts/measure_pv_performance_ratio.py:110, simulate_pv_output at :126). Ageing on AC after the inverter clips is the wrong place (live task 284, documented in docs/pv-system-losses.md §7), and apply_degradation has no other caller once that is fixed (live task 609). finance.py computes its own pv_soh from calculate_degradation_factor in parallel. The derating policy has no single home.
findings.proposal: Make the model chain the single owner of DC derating. Fold the degradation factor into the losses step as kept_fraction = (1 - system_losses) * calculate_degradation_factor(config.system_age_years, config.degradation_rate_per_year), computed in one named function that both the chain and finance's SOH display call. simulate_pv_output shrinks to run, convert W to kW and clip. Then delete apply_degradation (609) and the after-the-fact multiply (284), and give every consumer of create_model_chain the same physics. Task 284 and 609 are symptoms; this is the structure that produced them.
findings.bug_history_link: live tasks 284 (ageing after clipping) and 609 (apply_degradation orphaned); fix(332) one home for degradation invariant; task 252 system losses
findings.verdict_notes: pv.py::_deduct_system_losses is the chain's losses_model (DC side). simulate_pv_output clips and then calls apply_degradation on AC after the chain. finance.py computes pv_soh from calculate_degradation_factor. scripts/measure_pv_performance_ratio.py uses create_model_chain (line 110) and simulate_pv_output (line 126). Task numbers are not checkable here.

findings.title: 'The DC the model wires' is re-derived and validation still uses three capacity bases
findings.statement: After tasks 239 and 324, validation's annual-yield and peak checks divide by wired_dc_capacity_kw(config). That function calls _module_parameters and _module_count itself rather than reading what _pv_system built, so the wired DC and the actual PVSystem agree only because two call sites run the same helpers; nothing stops a new input to the sizing from reaching one and not the other. The fix stopped at two checks: validate_simulation still passes pv_config.capacity_kw (nameplate) to validate_self_consumption_pv_only and validate_self_consumption_with_battery, which use a hard-coded `capacity_kw * 900` 'rough UK yield' in their exception messages. That figure belongs to neither the 300-1200 band nor the measured ~1000 kWh/kWp. cli/validate.py `results --pv-kw` rebuilds a default PVConfig from a number to guess the wired DC of a CSV. finance.py::compute_project_economics prices capex on nameplate capacity_kw. The same quantity (the PV array's size) thus has three definitions, the same drift class as tasks 239 and 324.
findings.proposal: Introduce a frozen PVDesign in pv.py (module parameters, module count, wiring, inverter) built once by design_pv(config, candidates). _pv_system(design) builds the PVSystem from it, and design.dc_kw is the one wired DC. wired_dc_capacity_kw becomes design_pv(config).dc_kw, and validate_* take the design's dc_kw (or the PVConfig and call it once) in every check. Move the 900 kWh/kWp figure and the 10% peak margin into named constants beside the yield band in validation.py, or delete the exception-message heuristics. State once, in PVDesign, which size finance prices on. This removes the two-helper coincidence and the nameplate-versus-wired split, and would have prevented 239 and 324.
findings.bug_history_link: fix(239) annual-yield check divides by the DC the PV model wires; fix(324) validation judges per wired DC, peak allows 10% over
findings.verdict_notes: wired_dc_capacity_kw re-calls _module_parameters and _module_count rather than reading what _pv_system built. validation.py::validate_self_consumption_pv_only and validate_self_consumption_with_battery take capacity_kw and use the hard-coded capacity_kw * 900. validate_simulation passes pv_config.capacity_kw to them. cli/validate.py builds PVConfig(capacity_kw=pv_kw). finance.py prices on home.pv_config.capacity_kw. The 'three definitions' wording is somewhat loose.

findings.title: PVConfig is rebuilt field by field in several places, each dropping a different subset
findings.statement: _modify_pv_config constructs a new PVConfig in three branches, each copying ten named fields. It omits custom_module_params, custom_inverter_params and system_losses, so a sweep over pv_capacity_kw, pv_tilt or pv_azimuth silently resets them. generate_homes_from_distribution builds a PVConfig from sampled values and drops temperature_coefficient, inverter_capacity_kw, name and system_losses. _PV_BLOCK_KEYS is a third hand-kept field list. scenario_writer's pv block raises for custom parameters but writes no system_losses and does not refuse a non-default one, so a PVConfig with system_losses=0.2 round-trips to the 0.1408 default with no error (the YAML exposure is task 283, but the silent drop is independent of it). A new PVConfig field (system_losses is the latest) needs edits at each site, and the compiler does not flag the sites that miss it. Other callers use dataclasses.replace (cli/home.py, web/fleet_config.py), so the mechanism already exists.
findings.proposal: Replace the three manual constructions in _modify_pv_config with dataclasses.replace(config, capacity_kw=value). Declare once, next to PVConfig, which fields the scenario grammar can express, as a tuple of field names. Derive _PV_BLOCK_KEYS, the scenario_writer dict and the distribution field list from it, and have the writer refuse a non-default value for any field outside it, as it already does for custom_*. Add a test that enumerates dataclasses.fields(PVConfig) against that tuple, so a new field forces a decision. Doing this together with task 283 prevents the next 'field not carried' defect.
findings.bug_history_link: speculative; adjacent to live task 283 (system_losses exposure) and the 195 ignored-fields defect
findings.verdict_notes: Three branches each rebuild PVConfig from ten named fields. They omit custom_module_params, custom_inverter_params and system_losses. generate_homes_from_distribution (~line 1711) drops temperature_coefficient, inverter_capacity_kw, name and system_losses. scenario_writer::_pv_block refuses custom params but ignores system_losses, which pv.py::PVConfig has as a field, and config.py has no system_losses handling. So a non-default system_losses is silently lost on write.

findings.title: get_tmy_data reads a module-global WeatherCache, and fleet compensates by pre-fetching in the parent
findings.statement: get_tmy_data(location, use_cache) fetches its cache from the process-global _weather_cache through get_weather_cache()/set_weather_cache(). The cache is therefore an implicit input, a temporal coupling on a prior set_weather_cache call, and it does not cross a process boundary under spawn or forkserver. Task 460 (workers ignored the injected cache, read .cache/weather and fetched PVGIS) is the symptom, and it reproduces only on the interpreter-matrix lane. The fix compensates in a different module: fleet._tmy_by_location fetches one TMY per location in the parent and passes it down as weather_data, and simulate_fleet_iter's docstring explains why workers must not read the cache. Scripts, tests/conftest.py and measure_mppt_window.py mutate the global to inject a cache. Any new process-spawning caller can reintroduce the bug.
findings.proposal: Make the cache an explicit argument: get_tmy_data(location, *, cache: WeatherCache | None = None), with the process default resolved only at the top-level entry points (CLI, web, public facade). Keep get_weather_cache/set_weather_cache exported, because they are in the frozen API, but have them only supply the default. Tests and scripts then pass a cache instead of mutating the global. The parent-side pre-fetch in fleet stays as an optimisation but stops being a correctness requirement. A test that runs a fleet under each start method with a seeded cache pins it.
findings.bug_history_link: task 460 (spawn/forkserver workers ignore WeatherCache; fix pre-fetches in the parent); task 285 key-version bump
findings.verdict_notes: weather.py has a module-global _weather_cache behind get_weather_cache/set_weather_cache, and get_tmy_data (~line 323) reads it implicitly. scripts/measure_mppt_window.py:608 and scripts/measure_pv_performance_ratio.py:209 call set_weather_cache. The fleet.py pre-fetch compensation was not opened line by line; its docstring at line 328 references the cache installed with set_weather_cache.

findings.title: WeatherCache stores one frame as two files with stringly-typed timezone and frequency
findings.statement: An entry is a CSV plus a JSON sidecar. Round-trip fidelity relies on str(index.tz) being a name pandas can resolve (put refuses zones whose str names none, via _require_timezone_name) and on freqstr round-tripping through asfreq. The sidecar is written with prefix, latitude, longitude, start_date and end_date, none of which get reads; get reads only timezone and freq. If the CSV exists but the sidecar is missing, get silently returns a frame parsed by parse_dates=True with no timezone, a different type from a normal hit. The put docstring concedes that two os.replace calls are atomic only 'while every put under one key stores the same timezone and frequency'. Task 464's two fixes (UTC-then-convert, round_trip floats) and the amend added _require_timezone_name are each a patch for a place where text stood in for a typed index. The cache has also moved key versions (task 285).
findings.proposal: Store one self-describing file per entry so the single os.replace covers the whole entry and the sidecar disappears: for example a format that records the index as UTC instants plus the timezone name in the same file (parquet would do this directly, but pyarrow is only in the web extra, so check before choosing). Parse into a frozen CachedFrameMeta (timezone, freq) at the boundary; get then returns either a typed frame or a miss, never a degraded frame. Drop the unread metadata keys, and with them _require_timezone_name's round-trip gate if the format stores the zone key rather than its str.
findings.bug_history_link: fix(464) WeatherCache round trip (1a3034a, 778f3d1) and the follow-up amend refusing unrestorable timezones; feat(461) atomic put
findings.verdict_notes: WeatherCache.get does return a tz-naive frame when the CSV exists without its sidecar, and reads only timezone and freq from the sidecar. Real, but that state arises only from a partial write or manual deletion, and put replaces atomically. _require_timezone_name already guards the unrestorable-timezone case. Low consequence, so the claim is overstated.

findings.title: _module_rating_w falls back to 400 W for PVWatts modules without STC, so the wired DC differs from what pvlib models
findings.statement: _module_rating_w returns module_params.get('STC', 400.0). create_simple_module_params writes both pdc0 and STC, so the library helper is consistent. But custom_module_params of the form {'pdc0': 300, 'gamma_pdc': -0.004}, which _inverter_and_wiring accepts as PVWatts parameters (via _PVWATTS_MODULE_KEYS), have no STC. The module count is then round(capacity_kw*1000/400) while pvlib's PVWatts DC model scales each module by pdc0 = 300 W. The modelled DC and wired_dc_capacity_kw's count*400 W disagree, and a 4 kW config models 3 kW of modules while validation reads 4 kW. No error is raised. (Computed from the code; not run, since pvlib is not installed in the review environment.)
findings.proposal: Resolve the rating from the parameter set that the DC model actually reads: pdc0 when the PVWatts keys are present, STC otherwise, and raise (naming the missing key) when neither exists, instead of defaulting to 400. Put it in the module-spec resolver of finding 1, so that count, wired DC and the chain all see the same number.
findings.bug_history_link: speculative; same family as fix(196) (custom PVWatts module chain) and fix(324)
findings.verdict_notes: _module_rating_w returns module_params.get('STC', 400.0). _inverter_and_wiring accepts any module params that contain the PVWatts keys, with no STC requirement. _module_count therefore divides by 400 W even when the module has a different pdc0, so the wired count and wired_dc_capacity_kw disagree with what pvlib's PVWatts model scales. No error is raised. The probe was not run; this is traced from the code.

findings.title: Location accepts a non-finite altitude and an unvalidated timezone until a model chain is built
findings.statement: Location.__post_init__ checks `self.altitude < -500`, which is False for NaN, so altitude=nan passes (and inf passes by design); the same sequence of range checks is not written to refuse non-finite values the way PVConfig's was after task 332. timezone is any string: a typo such as 'Europe/Londn' is accepted at construction and fails only inside PVLibLocation in create_model_chain_picking_from, or later in the load profile's tz handling, far from the config that caused it. Locations are the cache key input for fleet._tmy_by_location and WeatherCache._make_key. This is the 'checked in some constructors and not others' pattern PVConfig had.
findings.proposal: In Location.__post_init__, require math.isfinite on altitude and validate the timezone with zoneinfo.ZoneInfo (error naming the field and value), so that the construction and use points both agree. A unit test over (nan, inf, -inf) for every float field closes the class.
findings.bug_history_link: speculative; same class as fix(332) PVConfig non-finite
findings.verdict_notes: __post_init__ checks latitude and longitude with not -x<=v<=x (so NaN is rejected), but altitude only with 'altitude < -500', so NaN passes. timezone is never validated; the only checks are on latitude, longitude and altitude.

findings.title: A chart's identity, title, height, emptiness and draw call are stated four times with no single description of a chart
findings.statement: Each chart on a results page is described in four unrelated places. (1) routes.py::home_results builds a dict keyed by chart name, whose values are JSON strings. A builder returns '{}' (sankey_diagram, sweep_parameter_chart), None (monthly_summary, seasonal_comparison, heat_pump_analysis) or JSON, so 'nothing to draw' is a three-state string convention (heuristic 12). (2) results/home.html and fleet.html guard each container with `{% if charts.x and charts.x != '{}' %}` and hand-write the card, an h3 title, `id="chart-..."` and `style="min-height: NNNpx"`. The title and height repeat what the Python builder already sets in `fig.update_layout(title=..., height=...)`. (3) The inline script repeats the id in `renderChart('chart-...', ...)`, with a separate and different guard (`{% if charts.monthly %}`, or none at all for chart-financial). (4) chart-renderer.js::renderChart re-checks `jsonStr === '{}'` and then the missing element. The chart_container macro, which bundles card, title, id and height, exists but only history/compare.html uses it (results/home.html has 9 hand-written panels, fleet.html 5). The id-written-twice rule is policed by tests/unit/test_web_results_chart_targets.py, which regex-reads the page's script via tests/_html_page.py::render_chart_targets. Its docstring concedes the converse (renderChart called for a container the guard omitted) is unchecked. The drawing seam is also not single. Results pages use renderChart. compare.html calls Plotly.newPlot itself (see the separate finding). The sweep page's JS `_renderChart` draws with Chart.js, which no template loads. It reads `document.getElementById('sweep-chart')` as a canvas, but sweep.html makes that element a <div>, so the call returns at `typeof Chart === 'undefined'`. charts.py::sweep_parameter_chart, the Plotly equivalent, is called only from tests/unit/test_web_scenarios.py. The Plotly CDN script tag is repeated verbatim in three templates, and results/home.html and fleet.html each also load chart-renderer.js. Measured: three draw paths, one id written 2-3 times per chart, and the same emptiness rule written in Python, Jinja (x2) and JS.
findings.proposal: Introduce one typed description of a chart, e.g. `ChartPanel(slug, title, height_px, figure_json)` (frozen dataclass), in charts.py or a new web/chart_panels.py. Each builder returns a figure or None, never '{}'. A page assembler (`home_chart_panels(results, summary, config) -> list[ChartPanel]`, `fleet_chart_panels`, `comparison_chart_panels`) returns only the charts that have something to draw, grouped by tab. The route passes that list. One Jinja partial, `chart_panels(panels)`, loops it and renders chart_container and the single `renderChart(slug, figure)` call from the same record, so the id, title and height live once and the emptiness rule is 'not in the list'. Pull the Plotly + chart-renderer.js script tags into one `{% block chart_scripts %}` or partial that every chart page includes (this also closes the CDN duplication tasks 129/250). Delete: the `!= '{}'` guards, the `'{}'` returns, the JS `'{}'` check, the hand-written panels, the inline renderChart blocks, tests/unit/test_web_results_chart_targets.py and `render_chart_targets`/`render_chart_figure` regex readers, and the dead Chart.js sweep path or the Python sweep chart (whichever the sweep page keeps). Prevents the id-twice, empty-figure-rule and missing-container classes (637, 674, 639, 635, 683) and the unwired sweep chart (123, 135).
findings.bug_history_link: live tasks 637, 674 (chart id written twice), 639 (empty-figure rule in JS and every template), 635 (renderChart logs missing target id; 7280eee), 683, 123/135 (sweep chart unwired), 129/250 (Plotly CDN tag duplicated); done: f8dafa1 fix(232) chart_container height
findings.verdict_notes: results/home.html: each chart guarded by `charts.x and charts.x != '{}'`, hand-written id/min-height, then renderChart('chart-...') repeated in script. charts.py returns '{}' (lines 294, 1006) or None. compare.html uses chart_container; results pages do not. sweep.html:201 makes sweep-chart a div, parameter-sweep.js:_renderChart expects a canvas and Chart.js, no template loads Chart.js; sweep_parameter_chart has no src caller. Plotly CDN tag appears in 3 templates.

findings.title: The dashboard palette has no single home: theme, chart palette, chart theming and status colours are separate and mirrored by hand
findings.statement: Colour is defined in at least five places that tests must keep reconciled. (a) tailwind.config.js `primary` is a verbatim copy of Tailwind's built-in amber (its comment says tests rely on that). Accent and status roles therefore share the same classes, and tests/unit/test_web_theme_colours.py needs a 316-line allow-list (_AMBER_ROLES: 5 roles, per-template class sets) to tell an accent use of bg-amber-500 from a status use. Tasks 235, 343 and 539 each fixed one instance of this. (b) charts.py::COLOUR_PALETTE is a separate palette whose `_AMBER = '#f5a623'` differs from primary-500 `#f59e0b`, and a few chart colours are outside it ('#888888' annotation, 'black' Sankey outline). (c) chart-renderer.js hard-codes the card surface and text colours (`#1e293b`, `#e2e8f0`, `#334155`, `#ffffff`, `#e2e8f0`) that mirror Tailwind slate classes on the card in macros.html, so a theme or card edit reaches the page but not the chart. (d) parameter-sweep.js writes '#f59e0b' and '#6b7280' literally; test_web_theme_colours.py's hex checks explicitly skip scripts. (e) run-status colours exist in macros.html's `_run_status_badge_classes` dict, again as bg-green-500/bg-amber-500 in progress-tracker.html, and as an if/elif on flash category in base.html, with statuses as bare strings in JS ('queued', 'pending', 'completed', 'failed'). The Python side already has the typed vocabulary (database.py RunStatus/JobStatus Literals), but the templates and JS key on string literals, so 'queued' silently falls to the neutral badge. The invariant 'the palette is defined once' is enforced only by tests that regex-scan source text, with documented holes.
findings.proposal: Make the theme tokens the one home and have everything else read them. In tailwind.config.js, define semantic status tokens (`status.pending|running|completed|failed`, plus `surface`) as a separate palette from `primary`. Expose them as CSS custom properties in static/src/input.css (`:root`/`.dark`). Then: macros.html badges and progress-tracker.html use `bg-status-*` utilities, which kills the need for _AMBER_ROLES, the amber-copy premise test and per-template class lists. chart-renderer.js takes its surface/text/grid colours from `getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).getPropertyValue('--chart-surface')` instead of hex literals, and parameter-sweep.js (or its replacement) reads the same variables. Generate COLOUR_PALETTE's accent/status entries from the same token file (a small JSON read by both tailwind.config.js and charts.py) so the chart palette derives from the theme or is explicitly a different thing. Deletes: _AMBER_ROLES and its 4 guard tests, the 'copies amber' premise check, the JS hex literals, the duplicated status mapping in progress-tracker.html. Prevents the 235/343/539/356/537/342/348 class.

findings.verdict_notes: charts.py _AMBER='#f5a623' differs from the primary '#f59e0b' that parameter-sweep.js writes literally. chart-renderer.js hard-codes #1e293b in _darkOverrides. The multi-place palette claim holds; I did not count every detail (316-line allow-list, status badge duplicates).

findings.title: charts.py re-derives engine facts (PV vs grid charge, whether a tariff is configured, SOC limits) because results do not hand them over typed
findings.statement: The upstream subsystem is the engine's results layer (home.py SimulationResults/SummaryStatistics, with flow.py). The engine partitions battery charge per timestep: flow.py computes pv_charge_stored_kwh and grid_charge_stored_kwh. SummaryStatistics keeps only one part (total_grid_charge_kwh, whose invariant is enforced in __post_init__) and the totals that include it. The web layer reconstructs the rest. Sankey: sankey_diagram computes `pv_to_battery = total_battery_charge_kwh - grid_charge`, `pv_to_demand = total_self_consumption_kwh - total_battery_discharge_kwh` and `grid_to_demand = total_grid_import_kwh - grid_charge`, which depends on the unstated fact that self-consumption includes battery discharge. Radar: comparison_radar computes 'Battery Utilization %' as `total_battery_charge_kwh / total_generation_kwh`, which does not subtract grid charge. The two charts therefore disagree on the same quantity (task 492; 628 'derived twice'), and fix(469) existed because Sankey previously missed the split. Tariff: `_unpriced_import_note` decides whether a run was priced from `results.tariff_rate.gt(0).any()` and `export_revenue.gt(0).any()`. financial_breakdown's own docstring admits 'SimulationResults records the import tariff's rate but no export rate, so the chart cannot tell [an SEG run that exported nothing] from a run with neither'. That is a chart compensating for a missing engine guarantee. It took three commits plus an amend (76e576d, fba34ca, 1de43b4) to settle. SOC limits: battery_soc_chart takes a BatteryConfig and instantiates a Battery just to read min_soc_kwh/max_soc_kwh. fix(645) found the previous hard-coded 10%/90%. The limits are a fact of the results, not of a config the route must re-supply (routes.py::home_results passes `config.battery_config` and re-guards `has_battery and config.battery_config is not None`).
findings.proposal: Move the facts into the results types where the invariant already lives. On SummaryStatistics add derived read-only properties next to __post_init__, e.g. `total_pv_charge_kwh`, `total_pv_to_demand_kwh`, `total_grid_to_demand_kwh` and `battery_pv_utilisation_ratio`, with their identities documented once. Consider carrying `total_pv_charge_kwh` itself from flow.py. sankey_diagram and comparison_radar both read these, which makes disagreement impossible. Add typed `tariff_configured: bool` and `seg_configured: bool` to SimulationResults (set where simulate_home already knows the tariff), so `_unpriced_import_note` becomes a lookup and the 'cannot tell' caveat disappears. Add `soc_limits_kwh: tuple[float, float] | None` to SimulationResults (or SummaryStatistics) so battery_soc_chart takes `results` only. Deletes: the subtraction arithmetic in sankey_diagram/comparison_radar, `_unpriced_import_note`'s inference and its long docstring, the BatteryConfig parameter and Battery import in charts.py, and the has_battery guard in routes.py. Prevents the 469/492/628/645/665 class. Note the frozen-API consumer: additions are additive properties/fields with defaults.
findings.bug_history_link: fix(469) b7fc96a; fix(645) 184fa62; fix(665) 76e576d/fba34ca/1de43b4; 4d48867 hardcoded tariff rates; live 492, 628
findings.verdict_notes: charts.py:281-283 derives pv_to_battery, pv_to_demand and grid_to_demand from totals minus grid_charge. comparison_radar computes battery utilisation as total_battery_charge_kwh/total_generation_kwh with no grid-charge subtraction, so the two charts disagree. The tariff-inference and SOC-limit sub-claims were not individually traced.

findings.title: Run-comparison charts read raw summary dicts with .get(key, 0), so a fleet run in a comparison silently charts as zeros
findings.statement: history.compare_page builds `runs` from `RunRecord.decoded_summary()` (a JSON blob decoded to `Any`, `{}` on failure) and passes `[r.get('summary', {}) ...]` to comparison_bar_chart and comparison_radar, typed `list[dict[str, Any]]`. Typed loaders exist (storage.load_home_run returns SummaryStatistics; load_fleet_run returns FleetSummary), but the comparison path bypasses them. The charts read `summary.get('self_consumption_ratio', 0)`, `'grid_dependency_ratio'`, `'export_ratio'`, `'total_battery_charge_kwh'` and the five `total_*_kwh` keys. compare_page does not filter by run type (compare.html renders `run_type_badge(run.type)`, so mixed or fleet runs are expected). A fleet run's stored summary is asdict(FleetSummary), whose keys are `fleet_self_consumption_ratio`, `fleet_grid_dependency_ratio` and no `export_ratio` or battery fields. The radar therefore draws 0 for those axes with no error. The `.get(..., 0)` default turns a schema mismatch into a plausible wrong chart (heuristic 10: informative failure). The broad `except Exception: logger.warning(...)` around chart construction in compare_page turns real exceptions into a 'No chart data available.' page, and the same function-local import of charts appears in routes.py (`# noqa: PLC0415` x2), with no import cycle to justify it (charts.py imports only engine modules).
findings.proposal: Define the comparison input as a typed value: `ComparableRun(label: str, summary: SummaryStatistics | FleetSummary)`, built in storage (a `RunStorage.comparable_runs(ids)` that deserialises with the existing `_deserialize_dataclass`) and failing with a named ValueError on an unreadable summary. Give both summary types the shared fields the comparison needs via one small protocol/property set (`self_consumption_ratio`, `grid_dependency_ratio`, `export_ratio`) so the fleet variant maps `fleet_*` fields once, in the type that owns them. comparison_bar_chart/comparison_radar take that typed sequence. Either refuse mixed run types in compare_page with a flash message or chart them correctly. Delete: the `.get(key, 0)` defaults, the stringly `summary_keys` table in comparison_bar_chart, the blanket try/except in compare_page, and the lazy chart imports.
findings.bug_history_link: speculative; adjacent to live 565/575 (summary-key tables duplicated) and 492 (radar battery utilization)
findings.verdict_notes: comparison_radar reads summary.get('self_consumption_ratio',0), 'export_ratio', 'total_battery_charge_kwh' with a 0 default. history.py::compare_page passes decoded_summary dicts with no run-type filter (runs.html checkboxes are offered on every row). A fleet summary uses fleet_self_consumption_ratio (fleet.py:236), so those axes silently read 0. compare_page's broad except Exception and its function-local import are as described.

findings.title: history/compare.html draws its charts with raw Plotly.newPlot, bypassing chart-renderer.js and its theme and hidden-tab handling
findings.statement: chart-renderer.js is documented as the shared Plotly renderer: dark/light layout overrides, deferred drawing of charts in hidden tabs via ResizeObserver, a theme-changed redraw. compare.html does not load it. Its script block calls `Plotly.newPlot('chart-comparison-bar', ...)` and `Plotly.newPlot('chart-comparison-radar', ..., {responsive: true})` directly inside DOMContentLoaded with its own try/catch and console.error text. charts.py::_SHARED_LAYOUT sets transparent paper/plot backgrounds and no font colour, so in dark mode the comparison charts get Plotly's default dark text on the slate-800 card (the contrast fix lives only in _darkOverrides). The toggle's `theme-changed` event has no listener on this page. The radar chart sits in a tab with `x-show="activeTab === 'radar'"`, so it is drawn while display:none, the exact case chart-renderer.js's deferral exists for (AC3). The page's tab buttons also lack the role=tab/aria-selected the results pages have. This is the invariant 'every chart goes through renderChart' held nowhere, which is why the draw path drifted. Not observed in a browser: the dark-mode contrast and hidden-tab sizing are read from the code paths.
findings.proposal: Load chart-renderer.js on compare.html and replace both inline Plotly blocks with `renderChart(id, figure)`, ideally via the shared chart-panel partial proposed in the chart-description finding. Then add one test that asserts no template calls `Plotly.newPlot` outside chart-renderer.js. Deletes the inline Plotly try/catch blocks. Prevents the dark-mode and hidden-tab chart bugs of the 683/691 class on the one page that escaped the fix.

findings.verdict_notes: compare.html:171-184 loads Plotly and calls Plotly.newPlot directly with no chart-renderer.js.
